name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,828

clue.text: Ship's officers make fast haul to port

definitions.note: The wardroom is the officers' mess in a warship, and the word stands for the officers who use it, as 'the bench' stands for judges.

indicators.note: Port is a ship's left-hand side, so each piece named is read back towards the left of the grid.

blocks.note: to haul something is to draw it, and DRAW read the other way is WARD
a ship is made fast by mooring it, and MOOR read the other way is ROOM

explanation.surface: An order on deck: tie her up and drag the load across to the left-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: One instruction serves both halves of the clue, which is why nothing is left over. Sailors moor a boat to make it fast, and the wardroom is where a warship's officers eat and sit.
explanation.definitionFit: The wardroom is the officers' mess on a warship, and naval talk uses it for the officers themselves.

clue.text: Stretching account with car purchase, one's sorry

indicators.note: Something stretched is pulled out at both ends, so the two letters named separate to leave room between them.

blocks.note: a/c is the everyday short form of account, and it is these two letters that pull apart
the Polo is Volkswagen's small hatchback
to purchase a thing is to get it
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A shamefaced admission about a car bought on the account, with the budget stretched to its limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretching' reads as the strained budget and is in fact the instruction. The car is the Volkswagen Polo, a favourite of setters for its four handy letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorry and apologetic are the same admission of fault, used both of the person and of the tone they say it in.

clue.text: Useful number mother used to get hold of trade union

indicators.note: To get hold of a thing is to take it into your grasp, so the letters before close round the ones after.

blocks.note: a dam is an animal's mother, the mare or ewe a young one is out of
TU is the standard short form of trade union

explanation.surface: A mother getting to grips with the figures her union has put in front of her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mother' is the breeder's word here: a dam is the female parent of a foal or a lamb. Datum is the forgotten singular of data.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is one given figure, the number a measurement or a calculation is worked from.

clue.text: Injury from fight with swords

blocks.note: of stands in for from in phrases like made of wood and made from wood
to fence is to fight with swords

explanation.surface: A duel with blades that leaves one of the pair wounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like the join between the wound and its cause, and is really the first two letters. The injury meant is the one done to a person's feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: An offence is an affront, the injury done to somebody's pride rather than to their body.

clue.text: A potentate so mad might become commonplace in America

indicators.note: 'Might become' says one set of letters is able to turn into another, which is what a shuffle does to them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A ruler driven out of his mind turns into something quite ordinary across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like the shuffling word and is part of the fodder instead, which is why the count comes out at fifteen. The phrase works as an adjective: a meat-and-potatoes job.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat-and-potatoes is chiefly American for the plain and basic, the everyday fare nobody thinks remarkable.

clue.text: Moth damaged by flame keeps back from candle

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, so these letters hold another letter inside them.
The back of a word is the letter it finishes on, and that single letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: anything damaged by flame has been burnt
the last letter of candlE

explanation.surface: A moth that has flown too near a candle flame and been singed.
explanation.walkthrough: The burnet is a day-flying British moth with crimson spots on dark green wings, common on chalk downs. 'Back from candle' reads as retreating from the flame and asks for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The burnet is a small day-flying moth, the red-spotted one seen over British grassland in summer.

clue.text: Things piled up in in-tray have nowhere to go, according to Spooner

definitions.note: A backlog is the heap itself, so the plural 'things piled up' describes the answer collectively rather than swapping word for word.

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so the phrase named trades its beginnings.

blocks.note: someone who lacks a bog — British slang for a lavatory — has nowhere to go, and the two opening sounds swap over

explanation.surface: Paperwork heaped in the in-tray with nowhere left to put any of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner clues work in sound rather than spelling, so say the answer aloud and trade the two openings. The lavatory sense of 'go' is what makes the phrase work.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is precisely the pile of work that has built up unattended in the tray.

clue.text: Check school during break

indicators.note: 'During' places one thing inside the span of another, so these letters sit within the ones named after it.

blocks.note: a break from work is a rest
to school somebody is to train them

explanation.surface: An inspector looking the school over while lessons are paused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is the verb, not the building: you school a horse or a pupil by training them. Check is the noun sense, the thing that holds something back.
explanation.definitionFit: A check is whatever holds something back, and restraint covers both the curb itself and the act of curbing.

clue.text: Land before crossing island

indicators.note: To cross a thing is to go over it from one side to the other.

blocks.note: ere is the old word for before
i = island, the abbreviation used on charts

explanation.surface: Reaching dry land before making the crossing over to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Ere is the poet's 'before' and a crossword regular. Eire is the Irish name of the Republic of Ireland, which is what makes the island in the surface so tempting.
explanation.definitionFit: Eire is the Irish-language name for the Republic of Ireland, a land in its own right.

clue.text: Rather like that ruined fort

indicators.note: A ruin has been knocked out of shape, and letters called ruined will not stand in the order they are given.

blocks.note: doing it like that is doing it so
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: Pointing at a tumbledown fort and saying this other thing looks much the same.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the last four letters move; the first two are handed over as they stand. Sort of and rather are both the English way of half-committing to a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: Sort of and rather are both hedges that soften whatever follows them: rather good, sort of good.

clue.text: Line of railway on winding ascent

indicators.note: In an across answer one thing lies on another by following it.
A winding road never runs straight, and letters called winding do not run in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
ry is the timetable's short form of railway

explanation.surface: A railway line climbing a slope that twists as it goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' wants to be the railway and is the family sort instead, the line you descend from. Only the six letters of the slope move; the railway is added whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A line in the family sense is the string of forebears a person comes down from, which is their ancestry.

clue.text: Writer casting doubt on William the Conqueror's armour?

indicators.note: In an across answer one thing goes on another by following it, so the two letters before it end up at the back.

blocks.note: William the Conqueror was a Norman, duke of Normandy before he was king, so he is one example of the word
mail is armour of linked metal rings
er is the noise made by somebody hesitating, the sound of doubt on the page

explanation.surface: A scholar querying whether the armour on display really belonged to William the Conqueror.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the loose bit: William stands for Normans in general. Norman Mailer wrote The Naked and the Dead and won two Pulitzers.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Mailer was an American novelist and journalist, so 'writer' is the plain trade of the man named.

clue.text: Son clumsily walking in sleep

definitions.note: The answer is a participle where 'sleep' is a bare noun; 'in sleep' names the state that slumbering describes.

blocks.note: s = son, as family trees abbreviate it
someone lumbering along moves with a heavy, clumsy walk

explanation.surface: A boy blundering about the house without ever waking up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clumsily' looks like a shuffling word and is part of the meaning instead: a lumbering walk is a heavy one. The s for son comes from the family tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Slumber is the older and gentler word for a quiet, untroubled rest, which is what the sleeping child in the clue is having.

clue.text: Clergyman's runs at some point stop

blocks.note: r = runs on a cricket scoreboard
at some point or other is ever
to stop a thing is to end it

explanation.surface: A vicar's innings finally comes to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket keeps the surface at the crease and supplies the opening letter. Reverend is a title that British speech turns into a noun for the man who holds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman is addressed as Reverend, and everyday speech lets the title stand in for the man himself.

clue.text: I peed next to doctor for convenience

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with do not stay as they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to relieving themselves beside the doctor because it was handy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public convenience is a lavatory, and that is the sense the surface wants. The definition is the other one, and 'doctor' is the medical word doing non-medical work.
explanation.definitionFit: An expedient is a handy means to an end, a convenience in the sense of whatever suits the moment.

clue.text: Horrible king who succeeded Anne by scheming

blocks.note: Queen Anne was followed on the throne in 1714 by George I, and a King George signs himself GR for Georgius Rex, so his name and number are GRI
somebody scheming is sly

explanation.surface: A Hanoverian king remembered as both horrible and underhand.
explanation.walkthrough: Grisly is the gruesome one; grizzly with a z is the bear, and the ear cannot tell them apart. Anne died in 1714 without a surviving heir and the crown went to Hanover.
explanation.definitionFit: Something grisly is horrible in the sickening, blood-and-bones way a newspaper means when it describes a murder scene.

clue.text: Cheap writer pockets 10p; that's life, you see

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it, and it splits the same way the word does: a life, and something you watch.

indicators.note: To pocket a thing is to slip it inside, so these letters take the next ones in.

blocks.note: the Bic is the cheap disposable ballpoint pen
the figures 1 and 0 read as the letters I and O, with p for pence after them

explanation.surface: A badly paid hack picking up a small coin and putting it in his pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheap writer' is the biro, not the hack. Reading 10 as the letters I and O is a trick worth storing away, and a biopic really is bio plus pic: a life, on screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A biopic is a film telling a real person's life story, so what you see is the life.

clue.text: 50% chance most of heaven's white

definitions.note: White here is the noun of the wine list — a white, as ordered at a bar — rather than the colour.

indicators.note: Half of a word is 50% of it, and for a six-letter word that is its first three letters.
Most of a word is all of it but the last letter, one short of the whole.

blocks.note: the front half of CHAnce
heaven is bliss, and BLISS one letter short is BLIS

explanation.surface: An even chance that most of heaven turns out to be white.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word at the end. 'Heaven's' hides an is rather than a possessive, which is what makes the sentence read so smoothly past the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A white on its own means white wine, and Chablis is the dry white made in that corner of Burgundy.

clue.text: Obvious one's last in line for extra pay

indicators.note: Being last in a word means being its final letter, and that letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: something obvious is overt, out in the open
one's spells out as one is, which a speaker says of himself as I'm, and grids have no apostrophes
the final letter of linE

explanation.surface: The obvious candidate finds himself at the back of the queue for a bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' is the pivot: taken as one is, it becomes the speaker's own I'm. Overtime is both the extra hours worked and the money they bring in.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtime is the extra money in the packet for hours worked beyond the normal week, as well as the hours themselves.

clue.text: Big head - Caesarean, possibly

blocks.note: the head of an empire, the largest thing a ruler can be head of
the rulers of Rome took Caesar as their title, so one of the Caesars is one example of the answer

explanation.surface: A conceited man, and a hint at how he was delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to read 'big head' as bighead, the conceited sort, and the operating theatre hangs about behind 'Caesarean'. Both halves are definitions; no letters move.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the head of an empire, head on the grandest scale; and the Caesars were emperors, so a Caesarean is possibly one.

clue.text: First Lady unhappily married to Head of State?

definitions.text: First Lady unhappily married to Head of State?

blocks.note: on the surface the wife of an American president; here the first wife of the man who now wears the British crown, and Lady was her own title before the wedding

blocks.clueFragment: unhappily married to Head of State?
blocks.note: the marriage ended in divorce in 1996, and Charles became head of state only on his accession years later, which the question mark acknowledges

explanation.surface: An American president's wife trapped in a miserable marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: No letters change hands anywhere. 'First Lady' pulls you straight to Washington, and the title that matters is Lady Diana Spencer, the name she had before the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Diana Spencer was Charles's first wife and the marriage was famously wretched; he is now King Charles III, Britain's head of state.

clue.text: Imminent threat's close hours before alarm sounds

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer by its hours, plural, where night is one singular stretch of them.

indicators.note: The close of a word is the letter it finishes on, and that one letter is what is wanted.

blocks.note: something imminent is nigh, close at hand
the final letter of threaT

explanation.surface: A danger looming through the small hours until the alarm goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imminent' and 'close' both point at nearness, and only one of them is a synonym; the other is an instruction. The whole second half of the clue is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the stretch of dark hours that ends when the morning alarm goes off, which is the roundabout way the clue names it.

clue.text: One might look after the kids twice a year

definitions.text: One might look after the kids

indicators.note: 'Twice' asks for the same short form to be written out two times over.

blocks.note: p.a. is per annum, the Latin a payslip uses for a year
the same two letters again, as 'twice' asks

explanation.surface: A relative who takes the children off your hands a couple of times a year.
explanation.walkthrough: Per annum is the phrase behind those two letters, and the clue wants them written out again rather than doubled in place. Kids are goats before they are children.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is the nursery word for father, and the father is the one who might be left minding the children.

clue.text: Last defeat playing Real, two nil

indicators.note: Players never stay where they are put, and letters said to be playing take up a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
a nil score is written as a nought

explanation.surface: A football report: Real beaten two-nil in the last game of the run.
explanation.walkthrough: Real Madrid supplies the scoreline and the letters at once. Meeting your Waterloo is the idiom the definition uses, after the 1815 battle that finished Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: Your Waterloo is the defeat there is no coming back from, the one that ends the run, named for Napoleon's last battle.

clue.text: Get back home after concerning case of gonorrhoea

indicators.note: 'After' sends the letters before it to the back.
A case is what encloses a thing, so only the outside letters of the word are wanted.

blocks.note: re is the memo's concerning, as in re: your letter
the outside letters of GonorrhoeA
somebody at home is in

explanation.surface: Getting home again after a worrying dose of an unpleasant infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' reads as worrying and is the filing clerk's re. The case wanted is the container sort, the outside of the word rather than the patient.
explanation.definitionFit: To regain a thing is to get it back into your hands, the re- carrying the sense of back as it does in return.

clue.text: Spirit lives on after

indicators.note: In an across answer one piece sits on another by following it, so the word before 'on' ends up second.

blocks.note: past and after both mean later than: past midnight is after midnight
he lives is he is, the verb in its plain sense of existing

explanation.surface: A ghost that carries on long after the person has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The haunting is the misdirection: spirit is the drinks sense. Pastis is the aniseed apéritif of southern France, the one that clouds when water is poured in.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastis is a spirit in the bottle sense, the aniseed apéritif drunk all over southern France.

clue.text: Wandering sheep interrupts general's planning

indicators.note: To interrupt is to break in partway through.

blocks.note: an animal wandering loose is a stray
a teg is a sheep in its second year, a shepherd's word the crossword keeps alive

explanation.surface: A lost sheep blunders into the middle of the general's war planning.
explanation.walkthrough: Teg is the farmer's name for a yearling sheep and survives mostly in grids. Strategy belongs to the general and tactics to the officer fighting the day's battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Strategy is planning at the general's level, the overall shape of a campaign rather than the handling of one fight.
